questions.stem: At room temperature and pressure (RTP), what volume does one mole of any gas occupy?
questions.explanation: At room temperature and pressure (approximately 20°C and 1 atmosphere), one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³). This is the molar gas volume at RTP.

questions.stem: What is the formula to calculate the volume of a gas at RTP?
questions.explanation: Volume (dm³) = Number of moles x 24. This works because each mole of gas occupies 24 dm³ at RTP.

questions.stem: What volume would 2 moles of carbon dioxide occupy at RTP?
How many moles of gas are in 6 dm³ at RTP?
Why does one mole of any gas occupy the same volume at the same temperature and pressure?

options.text: Because all gas molecules are the same size
Because gas particles are so far apart that their individual size is negligible compared to the space between them
Because all gases have the same mass
Because all gas particles move at the same speed

questions.explanation: In gases, particles are very far apart and the actual size of the molecules is negligible compared to the spaces between them. So the volume is determined by the number of particles, not their size.

questions.stem: What volume in cm³ does 0.5 moles of hydrogen gas occupy at RTP?
questions.explanation: Volume = 0.5 x 24 = 12 dm³. Converting to cm³: 12 x 1000 = 12,000 cm³.

questions.stem: In the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, what volume of H₂ gas is produced from 0.1 moles of Mg at RTP?
questions.explanation: From the equation, 1 mole Mg produces 1 mole H₂. So 0.1 moles Mg produces 0.1 moles H₂. Volume = 0.1 x 24 = 2.4 dm³.
